content: The results of any analysis must be interpreted within the framework of the assumptions underlying the study. Approximately 50,000 new HIV infections occur annually in the U.S., a figure that has remained stable over the past decade. PrEP has been shown to reduce HIV incidence by about 50%, but its effectiveness depends on factors such as adherence to medication, the number and type of sexual partners, condom use, and the viral load of infected partners. Translating reductions in HIV cases into quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained involves complex modeling approaches. Juusola et al. (2012) conducted a dynamic model analysis to estimate the cost-effectiveness of PrEP among men who have sex with men (MSM) in the U.S. The study found that initiating PrEP in 20% of MSM could reduce new HIV infections by 13% and result in a gain of 550,166 QALYs over 20 years, at a cost of $172,091 per QALY gained. Expanding PrEP to a larger proportion of MSM would prevent more infections but at higher incremental costs, reaching $216,480 per QALY if all MSM received PrEP. Targeting high-risk MSM improved cost-effectiveness, with costs of approximately $50,000 per QALY gained for MSM with an average of five partners per year. However, providing PrEP to all high-risk MSM for 20 years would increase healthcare costs by $75 billion, with an incremental cost of $600,000 per HIV infection prevented. In Australia, a study by Anne et al. (2014) used a stochastic agent-based model to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of PrEP among MSM in New South Wales. Providing PrEP to 10-30% of the MSM population was projected to cost an additional $316-952 million over 10 years, with costs exceeding $400,000 per QALY gained compared to the status quo. Targeting MSM with more than 10 to 50 sexual partners within six months was more cost-effective, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) ranging from $8,399 to $11,575 per QALY gained for 15-30% coverage. The study concluded that targeting HIV-negative MSM in discordant regular partnerships is the most cost-effective strategy, though it would not have a large population-level impact. In India, Mitchell et al. (2012) explored the impact of sexual mixing patterns among MSM on HIV epidemic trends and the effectiveness of targeted PrEP interventions. Deterministic models showed that different mixing patterns had minimal impact on overall HIV prevalence trends but influenced group-specific outcomes. Introducing PrEP with 42% effectiveness and 60% coverage among certain MSM groups (e.g., receptive and versatile partners) was projected to have a similar overall impact across the MSM population, regardless of mixing patterns. Globally, the use of PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy has raised ethical and public health concerns. Fiercek (2013) highlighted the challenges of distributing antiretroviral medications to healthy populations for prevention when millions of HIV-positive individuals lack access to treatment. These concerns are compounded by cultural and epidemiological assumptions about sexual behavior and population classifications, particularly in resource-limited settings. In the U.K., Duncan and Duncan (2012) assessed the quality of online information about PrEP available to patients. They found that while most websites provided definitions and efficacy data, few referenced national guidelines or described current clinical practices in the U.K. The study emphasized the need for comprehensive and accessible patient information to prevent unsupervised use of PrEP, which could lead to drug resistance and risky sexual behaviors. Overall, while PrEP has demonstrated efficacy in reducing HIV transmission, its cost-effectiveness varies depending on the target population, adherence rates, and healthcare costs. Targeted strategies, particularly among high-risk groups, are more cost-effective but may not achieve large-scale population-level impact. Ethical considerations and the need for robust implementation frameworks remain critical to optimizing the public health benefits of PrEP.
